sections.html:
This western Missouri county borders the Kansas City region on the east, and Lexington is where the courthouse stands. Towns buyers know include Higginsville, Odessa, Concordia, Wellington, Waverly and Alma, and a piece of Oak Grove lies at the western edge. The July 2025 count was 33,531 people and 14,508 housing units. Owners hold 75.7% of homes. The median owned home is valued at $216,500, and gross rent is about $928.

Six public school districts extend into the county. Your bill prints the levy for yours, and prospective buyers will want to know which district it is.

You will find the Assessor in the courthouse at 1001 Main Street, Lexington. Weekday hours are 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM; the phone is (660) 259-6158 and the email is assessor@lafayettecountymo.gov. The Assessor's website hosts a free GIS map and sells an enhanced version by annual subscription, and personal property declarations can be filed online until May 1 each year.

The Collector of Revenue receives current and past-due real and personal tax on behalf of the county and each district with an approved levy, then sends the money out every month to schools, the library, fire districts and others.

sections.h2: How and when to pay a statement
sections.html:
Statements go out in early November and are payable the day they arrive. After December 31 they are delinquent. Without a statement by Thanksgiving, phone the Collector at (660) 259-6171.

A mailed payment counts if it is postmarked December 31 or earlier; anything postmarked later comes back unprocessed unless late fees are enclosed. A single check can cover every statement you hold, but partial or incorrect amounts are turned away.

Ways to pay a Lafayette County tax statement
Payment methodHow it works
WebsiteCollector's website
MailP.O. Box 365, Lexington, MO 64067, postmarked by December 31

The counter keeps weekday hours of 8:30 to 4:30, noon included. Closings near Christmas and New Year's are posted on the Collector's home page, and the county site lets you print a tax receipt.

sections.h2: Dates to know through the year
sections.html:
The county tax year follows a steady pattern, and a sale that falls on the wrong side of one of these dates can cost you.

  • May 1: online personal property declarations are due at the Assessor.
  • Second Monday in July: cutoff for filing with the county board of equalization.
  • August: the Collector's delinquent tax sale.
  • Early November: statements are mailed, payable at once.
  • Thanksgiving: if you have no statement by then, call the Collector.
  • December 31: the postmark deadline, after which bills are delinquent.

A house listed in late summer has a current-year bill that has not been mailed yet. Put the split in the contract, spelling out who pays and how it is prorated, and expect the statement to be addressed to whoever the Assessor's records show as owner at printing.

Real estate and personal property can arrive as separate statements. Every district with an approved levy shows up on them, which is why a school district, a fire district and the library each take a slice of one payment. The Collector divides the money among them each month, so no one of those bodies will fix your bill for you.

Check the acreage, address and owner name against your deed before paying. Any error is the Assessor's to fix, and it costs less to fix one before a buyer's title company spots it. Put each year's printed receipt in your sale file.

On April 2, 2025 the county commissioners adopted Ordinance #25-01, relying on Senate Bills 190 and 756 and section 137.1050 of Missouri law. The credit it creates applies to a senior's primary residence.

The Collector's page announces each application period, including when the 2027 one opens. If you applied and qualified before, you do not file again. A new applicant uses the application form on that page, and a FAQ explains renewals. Read that FAQ before a sale to learn how a change of residence affects the credit.

Open with a conversation with the Assessor. When it fails, file with the county board of equalization by the second Monday in July at the latest. After the board, the State Tax Commission takes appeals filed within 30 days of the board's letter date.

The Commission also allows payment under protest. Send the whole amount to the collector by December 31, label it a protest, and include a written statement of your reasons and your idea of market value. If you bought less than 30 days after the county mailed the statement, or never heard about an increase, you may skip the board and go straight to the Commission.

Corporations, LLCs, trusts, estates and limited partnerships need an attorney to file.

Every August the Collector runs a sale of delinquent real estate. Missouri's tax sale rules are in Chapter 140 of the state statutes, and the winning bidder receives a certificate of purchase rather than an immediate deed.

Call the Collector for this year's date, the list of parcels and the amount needed to take yours off it, and ask which tax years put a parcel on the list.

When more than one year is open, ask the Collector to break the balance out by tax year. Seeing each year on its own helps you decide whether to pay ahead of listing or let the closing handle it, and it keeps a surprise year from appearing on the settlement statement. A seller who closes first avoids the sale altogether. The title company can pay the open balance from the proceeds at closing.

sections.h2: What to gather before selling a house that owes tax
sections.html:
Pull together a current statement and a written payoff from the Collector, and make sure both the real estate and personal property accounts are clear. Because the office refuses partial payment, the payoff has to cover the whole statement.

  1. Open the Assessor's GIS map and compare the acreage and address with your deed.
  2. Ask whether a senior credit applies and what a sale does to it.
  3. Print your paid receipt from the county site.
  4. Agree with the buyer on how the current year will be split.

Bring a copy of the payoff letter and the paid receipts to the closing so the settlement statement matches the Collector's numbers.

Selling for cash changes little here. The tax is still paid from the proceeds, but a buyer without a lender usually shortens the time between accepting an offer and getting the payoff cleared.

faqs.q: What is the last day to pay Lafayette County property tax without penalty?
faqs.a: December 31. The payment must carry a postmark on or before that date.

faqs.q: What phone number reaches the Lafayette County Collector?
faqs.a: Call (660) 259-6171, weekdays from 8:30 to 4:30. The mailing address is P.O. Box 365, Lexington, MO 64067.

faqs.q: Where is the Lafayette County Assessor's office?
faqs.a: In the courthouse at 1001 Main Street in Lexington. The phone is (660) 259-6158, and the email is assessor@lafayettecountymo.gov.

faqs.q: Will the Lafayette County Collector accept part of a bill?
faqs.a: No. Partial and incorrect payments are refused, although one check may cover all of your statements.

faqs.q: Is there a Lafayette County tax credit for older homeowners?
faqs.a: Yes, under Ordinance #25-01 for a senior's primary residence. The Collector's page announces the application period, including the one for 2027.
